newsitem.title: JAPAN: IMF move seen key to possible Thai rescue by Japan.
newsitem.headline: IMF move seen key to possible Thai rescue by Japan.

text.p: A possible move by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to help bail out Thailand will be the key to Japan's participation in a multibillion dollar Thailand rescue scheme, monetary sources said on Monday.

"Much depends on how Thai authorities judge the situation," an international monetary source said in reference to the possibility of the IMF opening a line of credit to Thailand. Bangkok currently does not have a loan programme with the IMF.
The source declined to comment on whether Japan's Export-Import Bank might follow suit if the IMF made such a move.
The fund has been offering technical assistance to the Bank of Thailand but sources said there are signs that the Thai authorities prefer to get primary support from Tokyo.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya arrives in Tokyo on Thursday for a two-day visit which he has said is aimed mainly at building ties with his Japanese counterpart.
Japan has stopped short of clarifying what sort of help it is ready to offer to Thailand.
"At first, we want to hear what their economic policies are, after their decision to float the baht and allowing it to fluctuate based on economic fundamentals," the source told reporters on Friday.

Thailand has said it would not rule out seeking financial assistance from the IMF to help solve its economic problems, which have been exacerbated since it decided to float the baht on July 2 and have triggered inflation and debt exposure worries.
An IMF technical team is in Thailand to help it manage the baht's flotation, but the fund has said are no plans so far on a new programme or a Mexico-style financial rescue package.
The U.S. Federal Reserve extended a short-term currency swap line to Mexico during the peso crisis of 1995 as a bridge to its long-term financing.

Thailand said last week it would try to raise a total of $10 billion, consisting of $5 billion in loans from banks and $5 billion in bond issues, in order to replenish reserves that were severely depleted when it defended its currency against speculative attacks in May.
A Japanese government official said Thailand may need both short-term and long-term loans.
Another monetary source said it may take a few more months before Thailand and the IMF reach a conclusion, if any, on a line of credit for Thailand.
Japan is technically able to extend loans to Thailand without the IMF's seal of approval, though such a move "may not be probable", another source said.
"It would be easier for the fund to generate the money for a country which already has an IMF-supervised programme, such as the Philippines," said the second source.

In order to set a programme, a country must agree with the IMF on its economic policy framework and structural reform, including tough conditions such as restraint on spending, an effort to balance trade and controlling inflation.
The Philippines, which has also gone through a de facto devaluation of its currency, is expected to be granted a $600 million package by the IMF soon.
It is still unclear whether Japan is ready to mobilise part of its external reserves, the world's largest at $222.305 billion as of July 1, to support Thailand.

Tokyo currency traders said Japan may set up a currency swap agreement with Thailand to mobilise part of those reserves, providing longer-term liquidity for Bangkok, rather than a so-called "repo" agreement.

In April of 1996, Japan agreed with the monetary authorities of Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand to establish bilateral repo or repurchase agreements to provide liquidity in times of currency crises. South Korea joined the pact in January this year.
The repo pact gives participants instant access to cash by selling their holdings of U.S. government securities to the pact's partners with a promise to buy them back later.
But the government official said the repo pact is designed for providing only short-term liquidity.
